How Good Are Copper Bullets, really???
Good read for those who hunt and are in states that ban lead ammo for hunting.

So, comparing apples to apples, the price of lead (by volume) is $27.34 per liter; copper costs $46.08 per liter. That doesn't account for the cost of obtaining new equipment for casting copper bullets. So one could reasonably expect the price of ammo to double, at least initially.

Only if by "ammunition" you mean "bullets." The price of bullets may double, but that doesn't equate to double the cost in powder, brass, primer and general labor - the overall change is very dependent on what round you're talking about but wouldn't approach 100%.

The thing is, copper bullets are ~7 times harder than lead bullets. See how little expansion there was to that projectile?

I don't believe there will be much more wear on the barrel, because most bullets are copper jacketed already. However, I can see this making it much harder to take large game, simply from an expansion standpoint.

Edited to add: Forgot to list my source info on the hardness: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brinell_scale

Lead 5 HB Aluminium 15 HB Copper 35 HB

You want that penetration for large game. Expansion doesn't help you if the bullet stops a couple inches in. It's why loads that are intended to take elk or bear are generally as heavy as possible and made out of hard cast lead or copper-jacketed lead.

I've been using copper bullets for quite some time for hunting and self defense and I've noticed that animals seem to drop a lot faster with the copper projectiles (especially the ones from Lehigh) versus traditional lead. That goes double for predators like coyotes.
I don't hunt or own a gun but this was fascinating to read!

Lately I have heard historians and people all over the world including America try to heap derision onto those responsible for the bombing and destruction of two cities in Japan using nuclear weapons. They say that it was unnecessary, barbaric, racist and America's holocaust. I think that they are raising an interesting and important question but I believe that they are completely wrong in coming to the conclusion that it was the wrong thing to do.

If I were to stand in judgement of President Eisenhower or Oppenheimer or any of the aircrew of the Enola Gay or indeed any of the hundreds of people who knew what type of terror they were about to release on the planet with Fat Man and Little Boy, I would say to them that theirs were the shoulders upon which the most significant decision of the 20th century fell and they miraculously did the right thing.

The deaths of what only God knows to be well over 250,000 people in Japan were not justified. Neither were the deaths of anyone in any theater of war in the history of mankind. I will not attempt to excuse the processes by which people choose to murder each other. What I want to talk about is the choices that were made in the context of the end of world war 2.

What is clear is that the atomic bomb was dropped with more than just the destruction of Japan and Japanese in mind. It was a deliberate and thoughtful attack by the Western allies on the Soviet Union, a show of force and will that brought about the cold war, which for all the terror it spawned, may go down in history as the least destructive international conflict between Great powers the world has ever known.

Japan was brought to heel and forced to surrender. They had already lost the war and they were suffering greatly on all fronts, yet they were still fighting in order to preserve the dignity of their emperor. These people had suffered massive civilian casualties in the firebombings that caused more destruction than the atomic bombs but they were still fighting. They were willing to surrender but not satisfactorily. They demanded that the emperor be allowed to maintain his seat on his own terms. This was unacceptable to the Allies because they knew that while they fully intended to reinstate him and they did so, nothing short of a full humiliation and destruction of the ruling class of Japan would suffice to convince the people to give up. It had to be the West that dominated because the Japanese had defeated the Russians in 1905 and considered them a foe they could defeat. They had on the other hand never yet defeated the forces of the west in a full scale conflict. If the Western Allies allowed Russia the time to re-mobilize to the east and invade Japan from the North they risked the type of invasion that was seen in eastern Europe with mass murder out of revenge for past defeats and the creation of a new Soviet state in Japan.

This was not a geopolitically advantageous position and with the knowledge that the USSR had every intention of expanding their sphere of influence as far as possible and knowing that one of the direct causes of the past world wars were ideological differences it was absolutely necessary to end the war as quickly and as dramatically as possible.

The victims in Japan were all as legitimate targets as the citizens of California, London, Berlin, Moscow, Leningrad or any other civilian population in the theaters. That is what total war is. We are extraordinarily lucky that we can't really understand what this means. Rationing, conscription, austerity, and the regular deaths of loved ones are the real consequences of an actual war. If Japan had developed the bomb first they would have used it where they could. The same can be said of Germany or Russia. We are extrodinarily lucky that the largest international coalition ever assembled, the Western Allies, were the group that eventually made the breakthrough. If they hadn't then only one group of people with only the interests of one Nation would have been responsible for making the decisions to use the weapon. We are lucky that the Western Allies Used the bombs in the most dramatically abhorrent way possible and then refrained from using them as General Patton wanted to against the Russians who were only two or three years from developing the same technology and under Stalin might have been much more likely to have used it had they been a victim of its use and not just a witness to the level of destruction it caused.

The fact that it is seen as racist is only a reaction to the fact that the USA and the Western Allies were racist at the time and only recently have begun to become less bigoted. At the time the Western Allies did think that the Japanese were lesser beings and that their deaths were less savage than the wholesale slaughter of white Germans. It doesn't change anything other than public perception of already racist people. Something that can cause destruction and force people to realize that they can die on that scale is one of the greatest egalitarian forces I am aware of. Shakespeare had his miserly Jew in the Merchant of Venice ask the potent question

"I am a Jew. Hath not a Jew eyes? Hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions; fed with the same food, hurt with the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, heal'd by the same means, warm'd and cool'd by the same winter and summer, as a Christian is? If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not laugh? If you poison us, do we not die? And if you wrong us, do we not revenge? If we are like you in the rest, we will resemble you in that."

Knowing that you can die the same way and with the same cruelty of any other man is the ultimate equalizer. The fact that Japan was more or less brought into the Western Alliance after the war speaks to the good intentions of the actions.

It was a holocaust but it secured what I like to call the 'pax atomica' that we enjoy today. I feel that given the same circumstances that existed during WW2 the only way to ensure that the war wouldn't continue for an unnecessarily long time and that the most beneficial outcomes would be achieved for the Western Allies who were unique in being the only Nation State not run as a dictatorship required the use of the Atomic Bomb against the Japanese. The questions that are raised by many historical revisionists and Western Apologists of mass murder, racism and barbarism are put to rest in the fact that the necessity of total war required that the atom bomb be used. It was a barbaric holocaust of mass murder justified by racism and cruelty, but it saved the world a much crueler fate and it was the right decision made by well meaning people who were trying to do the right thing.

If I were their judge, I would pardon them and let them live with the knowledge that as Oppenheimer said "I am become death, destroyer of worlds." But I'm not their judge and I still enjoy the benefits of the terrible awesome decision they made 70 years ago.
Dropping nuclear weapons on Japan was the right thing to do.
America could have just as easily done a show of force without wiping out countless innocent lives.

What makes you think that they were innocent? I'd wager that every single one of them had a personal stake in the success of Japan in the war. The Western Allies had to show a willingness to use the weapon against targets to cause maximum moral and economic damage. Those were the stakes of WW2 it wasn't a police action or a diplomatic spat like all subsequent wars between the great powers have been. This was total and complete cultural warfare on a scale that was only possible in the last two centuries or so.

I'd argue that in the context of WW2 there were absolutely no innocent bystanders outside of those few countries that maintained neutrality. If you contributed to the defence industries or the economy in anyway if you obeyed the rationing or had a loved one you gave material or mental support to who was fighting. Even if you chose to ignore the government's rules and disobey ration restrictions and dodge conscription or chose you were in some way acting as an agent of the enemy because in total war every engine of economic social and military power is fighting for self-preservation.

The German civilians who allowed the holocaust to occur were no less a legitimate target than the British subjects who dies in the London Blitz.

One more thing, the number of victims is not countless, more than 140000 and probably less than 500000 people died in the nuclear attacks. between 13 and 20 million people died throughout the course of the war and many more in the interwar and post war years as a direct result of the global struggle. What is countless and unknowable are the number of lives that were saved by the use of the atom bomb. It may be that more than the bare minimum of Japanese died because of the attacks but if you try to imagine a conflict between Joseph Stalin's USSR and the Western Allies that is one of the outcomes that the early and devastating end to the war was intended to bring then your math has to admit there are too many variables to be able to judge adequately.
